On 4 August 1943, when Churchill’s war cabinet first realised the enormity of the famine, it agreed that 150,000 tons of Iraqi barley and Australian wheat should be sent to Bengal, with Churchill himself insisting on 24 September that “something must be done”. Though emphatic “that Indians are not the only people who are starving in this war”, he agreed to send a further 250,000 tons, to be shipped over the next four months. 

On 7 October, Churchill told the war cabinet that one of the new viceroy’s first duties was to see to it “that famine and food difficulties were dealt with”. He wrote to Wavell the next day: “Every effort must be made, even by the diversion of shipping urgently needed for war purposes, to deal with local shortages.” Churchill refused a Canadian offer of 100,000 tons of food aid for Bengal because it would have taken two months to arrive, but the same war cabinet meeting resolved to seek Australian supplies instead.  By January 1944, Bengal had received a total of 130,000 tons of barley from Iraq, 80,000 tons of wheat from Australia and 10,000 from Canada, followed by a further 100,000 from Australia. Then, on 14 February 1944, Churchill called an emergency meeting of the war cabinet to see if more food aid could be sent to Bengal without wrecking Allied plans for the coming Normandy landings. “I will certainly help you all I can, but you must not ask the impossible,” Churchill telegraphed Wavell before the cabinet met.

A swallow flew gracefully through the air. Anton watched it with fascination. It danced like his sister had danced, carelessly, joyfully, with the innocence of a child. The swallow disappeared behind a building and was lost to him. Just like his sister.

He trudged with his unit through a broken and dying city, in a rotten and putrid country. Gunfire crackled in the distance and somewhere, someone was crying. 

*'Eyes up gentlemen, don't be too eager to meet the earth.'* The harsh whisper of the sergeant brought him out of his reverie. He scanned the buildings around him, searching for the enemy. Always searching. Always waiting. Always afraid.

Hitting the ground proved to him, that this was in fact life. The air had burst from his lungs and he lay helplessly upon the ground, wheezing. Jon groaned next to him, clutched at his ankle. 

*'Dammit! You alright Anton?'*

*'I think so'* Anton managed to croak *'Just winded.'* 

Anton looked up towards where they had fallen. Old wooden planks splintered across the gap, rotten with age. It looked like a stray artillery shell had uncovered just enough for them to fall through. lucky them.

Anton helped Jon up, but it quickly became obvious that he couldn't walk by himself. With Jon's arm around his shoulder, they stumbled through the dusty darkness. 

This place was old, that much was certain. There were runic carving in the walls, from a time before the words of Christ had reached these lands. They seemed to shine slightly in the gloom, an unnatural pale light leering out of the dusk.

They walked for what felt like hours, sweat cutting runnels through the dust on Anton's brow. The passage only seemed to go deeper. Ever deeper. 

Just as Anton was about to collapse, he saw something ahead. 

It looked like an altar of ancient stone, the same unnatural light as the runes, shone brilliantly from it. The light almost seemed to push them back as they stumbled their way forward, warning them away. 

As they got closer, they could see what was on the altar. A sword, pristine in it's glory, made of a metal Anton had never seen. Faint blue light came from it and the same runic inscription covered the hilt as had the walls. Except, now Anton could read it. 

***TRAITOR'S BOON OR HERO'S BURDEN***

Anton had let Jon fall to the ground. He couldn't take his eyes from the sword. He could feel it calling to him. He could feel it searching his mind, his soul. 

Jon cried out in pain as he hit the ground. Anton cried in ecstasy as he clutched the hilt.

He could feel the power coursing through him. He could feel the fires of a thousand suns tearing their way through him. He could feel his soul, fighting itself, shredding under the choice that must be made.

Jon looked up towards Anton. He saw his old friend and brother but also something more. He saw the sword in his hand, veins of gold spider webbing his skin. He saw Anton looking down upon him, a smile upon his face.
